pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Plants and animals in their habitats (needs–place model)

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-ESS3-1):** '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-1] or [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-1].'

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1, foundational to Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'):** precedes 'most living things live in habitats to which they are suited... how different habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals and plants' — this is the reception/Year-1 model-building step beneath it.

- **Operational details:** The youngest step: children USE A SIMPLE MODEL (a drawing, diagram, or matching layout) to represent WHY an organism lives where it does — connecting each need (food, water, shelter, suitable conditions) to a feature of the place. They match several organisms to their habitats with a reason, and predict what would happen if an organism were put somewhere its needs aren't met. The emphasis is on the MODEL as a representation of a relationship, not on naming many species.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, first modelling). Success = making/using a model that links an organism's needs to its habitat's features, matching at least three organisms to places WITH a need-based reason, and predicting failure in a mismatched habitat — not just pairing animal to place by looks.
bestPractices: Keep the model concrete, large and low-text — icons and pictures — for five-year-olds' first representation.
Always attach a REASON to each match ('the rabbit lives here because there's grass to eat and a burrow to hide in').
Use a mismatch/prediction move so the needs–place link is felt as consequence ('what if the fish were on the sand?').
Include plants as well as animals so 'needs and a place' isn't seen as an animals-only idea.
Let children build/draw their own simple model, not just read one, to meet the 'use a model' standard.
keyRepresentations: A two-panel needs→feature model (organism's need-icons linked to habitat features).
Organism-to-habitat matching cards with a spoken/drawn reason.
A 'droopy organism' mismatch cue showing an unmet need.
Simple habitat scenes (meadow, pond) with the resources highlighted.
commonMisconceptions: Matching animal to place by appearance rather than by needs met.
Thinking any animal can live anywhere.
Believing plants don't have needs or a place they are suited to.
Not connecting a specific need (water, food, shelter) to a specific feature of the place.
Seeing the picture as decoration rather than as a model of a relationship.

learn.summary: For 5-6 year-olds: use a simple model (drawing, diagram, or matching layout) to represent WHY an organism lives where it does, connecting each need (food, water, shelter, suitable conditions) to a feature of its habitat. Children build/use the model, attach a reason to each match, and predict what happens when an organism is placed where its needs aren't met. Includes plants as well as animals. Supports NGSS K-ESS3-1 and leads into UK KS1 'Living things and their habitats'.

activities.title: Connect the needs model: link each need to what the place provides
feedback: When a need is linked to the right feature, confirm it: 'yes - the pond gives the fish the water it needs to live in and breathe in'.
If a mismatch leaves a need unmet, make the consequence visible: 'the fish has no water here, so it could not survive on the sand'.
If the child matches by looks only, ask 'which need does this place actually give it?' to redirect from appearance to needs.
Praise a correct REASON, not just a correct pairing: 'you told me WHY - that's the model working'.
activities.rationale: The standard asks children to USE A MODEL of the needs-place relationship, so the child should build and manipulate the links rather than only view a finished picture. A live mismatch makes the relationship felt as a consequence. An optional interaction example: correct links can glow and a mismatched organism can visibly droop, making the unmet need concrete - this is one way to realise the mechanism, not a required feature.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-ESS3-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-1] or [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-1].'
learnerActions: Look at one organism (e.g. a rabbit) with a few large need-icons beside it: food, water, shelter, warmth.
Draw or drag a link from each need to the part of the habitat that provides it (grass to eat for food, a puddle or stream to drink from for water, a burrow to shelter in and keep warm).
Say aloud the reason for each link: 'the rabbit lives here because there is grass to eat and a burrow to hide in'.
Now try a mismatch: place a fish onto dry sand. Notice its water-need has nothing to connect to, so that link stays unmet and the fish cannot survive there.
Finally, build the model for a NEW animal or plant and say why its home suits it.
activities.intendedInsight: An organism lives where it does BECAUSE the place meets its needs; when a need cannot be met, the organism cannot live there.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal habitat reference: 'this place gives me...'
feedback: Affirm when the child names a real provided need: 'right, the meadow gives the rabbit grass to eat'.
If the child treats the scene as decoration, ask 'what does the rabbit GET from this place?' to recast the picture as a model of a relationship.
activities.rationale: A calm, pre-built reference presents the needs-place relationship for this age. Because it presents the model already made, it is a scaffold toward, not a substitute for, the child building and using the model themselves as the standard requires.
learnerActions: Tap an organism in a habitat scene (e.g. a rabbit in a meadow) and see what the place provides: grass to eat, a burrow to shelter, space to run.
Tap a fish in a pond to reveal what the pond gives it.
Say back, in your own words, one thing each place provides for that organism.
activities.intendedInsight: A habitat supplies specific things that match an organism's specific needs.

activities.title: Match organisms to habitats with a reason, and spot the missing need
feedback: If a match is made by appearance, ask which need the place actually supplies.
Reinforce naming the SPECIFIC missing need rather than a general 'it wouldn't like it'.
activities.rationale: Age-appropriate matching paired with a 'which need is missing?' follow-up checks the relationship, not just pairing by looks. Matching and picture-choice tasks elicit recognition; keep an open 'say or draw the reason why' step so the child constructs the explanation, which recognition alone does not require.
learnerActions: Match at least three organisms to the places where their needs are met (e.g. frog to pond, rabbit to meadow, cactus to desert).
For each match, give a need-based reason: 'the frog belongs here because the pond gives it water and insects to eat'.
For a mismatched pair, name which need is missing: 'this place has no water, so the fish's water-need is not met'.
Include at least one plant so the idea of 'needs and a suitable place' is not animals-only.
activities.intendedInsight: Matching is correct only when the place meets the organism's needs; a wrong place leaves a specific need unmet.

activities.title: Talking-animal prompt: 'where should I live, and why?'
feedback: Respond to the child's stated reason, extending 'because it likes it' into 'because it NEEDS the water the pond gives'.
If the reason is birthplace or preference only, prompt for the need the place supplies.
activities.rationale: An open talking prompt can draw out needs talk and reasoning. For first-time modellers at this age it may work well alongside a concrete visual model, where the needs-feature links can be shown rather than only discussed; no source establishes this format as more or less effective than the others.
learnerActions: Listen to an animal ask the child to pick its home.
Choose a place and explain which need each option would meet or miss.
Respond to a follow-up: 'what would happen to me if I lived in the wrong place?'
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing a home means reasoning about which needs a place can and cannot meet.

constraints: Keep the model concrete, large and low-text, using icons and pictures, for a five-year-old's first representation.
Always attach a REASON to each match; a pairing without a need-based reason does not meet the objective.
Include plants as well as animals so 'needs and a place' is not seen as animals-only.
Let children build or draw their own model, not only read a finished one, to meet the 'use a model' standard.
Picture-matching and picture-choice tasks elicit recognition; pair them with a spoken or drawn reason so the child independently constructs the explanation.
A tap-to-reveal reference presents the model pre-made; treat it as a scaffold, not as the child building/using the model.

Correct these errors directly during teaching: (a) an organism does NOT 'just get used to' or learn to survive in any place within its lifetime - moving it to a place that gives too little or too much of something it needs can stop it surviving; (b) organisms live somewhere because the place meets their needs, not merely because they 'like it' or were 'born there'; (c) plants DO have needs (water, light) and can get the wrong AMOUNT - too much water can make a desert plant's roots rot.

Mismatch reasoning can run both ways: too LITTLE of a resource (fish in the desert lacks water) and too MUCH (cactus in the pond gets more water than it can tolerate). Name the specific need and the wrong amount.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's diagnostic uses a double mismatch (fish to desert, cactus to pond). The correct answer rests on the cactus getting TOO MUCH water in the pond and the fish getting TOO LITTLE in the desert; ensure young learners are guided to the 'wrong amount / wrong conditions' idea, since a simple 'needs water = good' heuristic would wrongly predict the cactus thrives in the pond.
One source (NGSS) is marked verified:false in the row; the UK DfE source is verified:true. Treat the NGSS wording as quoted-but-unre-verified here.
The 'droop/glow' interaction is retained as an optional illustrative mechanism, not a mandatory or empirically tested feature.

No source claim establishes comparative efficacy of the interactive model over a static reference, dialogue, or matching; such comparisons in the original were catalog-fit judgements and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits.
The original probe examples (polar bear, camel) were not carried over verbatim; the transfer intent is preserved by the 'build the model for a new organism' step and can be extended with those pairs.
Feedback phrasing was adjusted from 'water it needs to breathe' to 'water it needs to live and breathe' to avoid implying fish breathe water itself, while staying age-appropriate.

probeDeeper: Why can a polar bear not live in your garden?
What does the fish get from the pond that keeps it alive?
Draw an arrow from the fish to the one thing in the pond it needs most, and tell me why.
A camel lives in the hot desert. What would happen to it in a cold, snowy place?
assess.correctAnswer: Both would struggle and die. The fish needs water to breathe and stay wet, so it dies in the dry desert; the cactus is built for very little water and would rot with too much in the pond. Each lives where it does because that place gives it what it needs — the right amount of water and conditions.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It would just learn to live there' — expects the organism to adapt to any place within its own lifetime.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Go back to what living things need to survive (prerequisite); a place only works if it supplies those needs — swapping them removes the need.
errorPatterns.distractor: The fish would be okay in the desert — it would just learn to live without water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the fish would be okay in the desert once it 'got used to it', or the cactus would be fine in the pond.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'They live there because they like it / were born there' — attributes the match to preference or birthplace rather than to needs being met.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe 'likes' as 'needs': the pond gives the fish the water it must have to breathe; ask what would be missing elsewhere.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the fish lives in the pond 'because it likes water' or 'because that's its home', with no need-based reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Plants don't really need anything' — thinks a plant, unlike an animal, has no needs, so a cactus would be fine anywhere.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that plants have needs too (water, light) and can get the WRONG amount; too much water harms a desert plant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the cactus would be fine in the pond because 'plants don't need much / don't mind'.

responseLevels.gap: Says each organism would 'get used to' the new place or lives somewhere just because it 'likes' it; cannot predict a mismatch.
responseLevels.full: Predicts both the fish and the cactus fail, names the specific need each new place gets wrong, and states the general rule that organisms live where the place meets their needs — transferring it to a new pair such as the polar bear or camel.
responseLevels.partial: Predicts one organism would struggle and names one need (the fish needs water), but does not reason about both, or does not tie the place to the need as a model.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a cactus (lives in the hot, dry desert) and a goldfish (lives in the pond). Ask: 'If I put the cactus into the pond and the fish out into the desert, what would happen to each one? Why does each one live where it does?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks living things 'just get used to' new places, or live somewhere merely 'because they like it', cannot predict the double mismatch. A child who links each organism to its needs predicts both fail and names the need that is wrong (too little water for the fish, too much for the cactus).
